newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Dixons gains from windfall spree.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Dixons gains from windfall spree.

text.p: Britain's biggest electrical retailer Dixons Group Plc on Wednesday said windfall cash from building society demutualisations was boosting sales of personal computers and major household appliances.

Chief executive John Clare said product sales had been strong across the board in the past two months, but the emphasis on big ticket items suggested people were spending cash received from the flotation of home loan groups such as the Halifax .
"It would be naive of us to believe that there wasn't an impact on these current trading numbers because this amount of money is coming into the consumer economy," he said in an interview

But Clare warned against reading too much into the group's current trading performance, which revealed a 17 percent increase in like-for-like sales in the first nine weeks of its 1997/98 financial year. The market had expected a more modest single figure increase.
He said recent rises in interest rates and expectations of another rise this week had to be taken into account.

"We've got to issue a little word of caution that these sales figures announced today are really after only nine weeks of the year and our most critical period is over Christmas and that's still a long way to go."

Clare said although the new Labour government's first budget last week did suck money out of the consumer economy, Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown himself had forecast growth in consumer demand of 4.5 percent this year and 4.0 percent next.
"If he's right it would suggest that the consumer economy is still likely to be strong."
The chief executive said Dixons had probably also benefited from unseasonal weather in June, which may have switched spending towards durables and away from fashion.
Personal computers had been selling well, cookers and cooking products, new technology products such as digital cameras, camcorders and hand held PCs.
He dismissed concerns that the PC boom, which has helped power Dixons recent profit growth, could slacken off.
He acknowledged there had been one or two bearish reports on the PC market largely because of problems in the United States. But he saw the market continuing to expand in Britain.
"I think that the PC market in this country is set to be a growing one for some considerable time."
He said tax breaks for small businesses in the budget, plus financial support for schools investing in technology, could help PC sales.
Sales at Dixons' PC World stores were up by 17 percent on comparable store basis in the year to May 3, 1997, driven by expansion of the PC market and new store developments.
The group's other stores Currys and Dixons also had a strong year. Currys' sales rose seven percent on a like-for-like basis, while Dixons sales were up six percent.
The Link, the mobile phone specialist in which Cellnet owns 40 percent, boosted sales by 17 percent stripping out new space.

Dixons reported a 41 percent increase in profits before exceptional items and tax to 190.2 million stg. It's shares surged on the results and current trading figures which were ahead of expectations. They stood 31 pence higher at 523.5 pence at 0825 GMT. -- Jane Merriman, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
